prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Simple examples are constructed that show the entanglement of two qubits being both increased and decreased by interactions on just one of them. One of the two qubits interacts with a third qubit, a control, that is never entangled or correlated with either of the two entangled qubits and is never entangled, but becomes correlated, with the system of those two qubits. The two entangled qubits do not interact, but their state can change from maximally entangled to separable or from separable to maximally entangled. Similar changes for the two qubits are made with a swap operation between one of the qubits and a control; then there are compensating changes of entanglement that involve the control. When the entanglement increases, the map that describes the change of the state of the two entangled qubits is not completely positive. Combination of two independent interactions that individually give exponential decay of the entanglement can cause the entanglement to not decay exponentially but, instead, go to zero at a finite time.

Simple qubit models examine how local interactions with an unentangled control qubit, including swap operations and combined decay processes, alter the entanglement of two noninteracting qubits. These interactions can reversibly transform maximal entanglement into separability and vice versa, with entanglement increases linked to non-completely-positive maps and combined exponential-decay channels causing finite-time entanglement loss.

outputs.L1: Simple examples are constructed to demonstrate that the entanglement between two qubits can be either increased or decreased through interactions involving only one of them. One qubit interacts with a third, control qubit that is never entangled or correlated with either qubit individually and never becomes entangled with them, although it does become correlated with the two-qubit system as a whole. The original two qubits do not interact, yet their joint state can change from maximally entangled to separable, or from separable to maximally entangled. Similar changes can be produced by a swap operation between one of the qubits and a control, in which case compensating changes in entanglement involve the control. When the entanglement increases, the map describing the change in the state of the two-qubit system is not completely positive. Moreover, combining two independent interactions, each of which individually produces exponential entanglement decay, can cause the entanglement to vanish at a finite time rather than decay exponentially.
outputs.L2:
Straightforward examples demonstrate that acting on only one member of a two-qubit pair can either raise or lower the pair’s entanglement. In these examples, that qubit couples to a third, controlling qubit. The control remains unentangled and has no correlations with either qubit individually, although it does develop correlations with the two-qubit system as a whole. Despite the absence of any direct interaction between the original pair, their joint state can shift from maximal entanglement to complete separability, or in the opposite direction.

Comparable transformations occur when one qubit is swapped with a control qubit; in that case, corresponding changes in entanglement involving the control offset the changes within the original pair. Whenever the pair’s entanglement grows, the map governing the evolution of its state is not completely positive. Moreover, combining two separate interactions—each of which alone produces exponential entanglement decay—can yield nonexponential behavior in which the entanglement vanishes after a finite time.
outputs.L3:
Interactions that act locally on only one member of a two-qubit pair can either reduce or increase the entanglement between the qubits. Although entanglement cannot increase under an isolated, completely positive local operation, an increase is possible when the qubit undergoing the operation is initially correlated with an additional control system. In that case, the effective reduced dynamics of the two qubits need not be completely positive.

A third qubit can serve as this control. It may remain unentangled with each of the two principal qubits when they are considered separately, while still developing correlations with the two-qubit system as a whole. These multipartite correlations allow the control qubit to influence how entanglement is distributed, even though it does not necessarily share pairwise entanglement with either qubit.

As a result, the two principal qubits can move between maximally entangled and fully separable states without interacting directly with one another. Swap operations between one of the principal qubits and the control provide a clear mechanism for this redistribution. When such a swap increases or decreases the entanglement of the principal pair, compensating changes occur in the entanglement or correlations involving the control, preserving the overall distribution of quantum information.

The mathematical description depends on the direction of the process. Entanglement-increasing reduced dynamics are represented by maps that are not completely positive, reflecting the presence of initial system–control correlations. By contrast, if the two qubits are each subjected to independent interactions that produce exponential decay, their combined effect can lead to “entanglement sudden death”: the pair’s entanglement reaches zero after a finite time, even though the individual local coherences or excitation probabilities may decay only asymptotically.
outputs.L4:
Simple qubit models provide a useful setting for studying how local dynamics can modify entanglement shared by two otherwise noninteracting qubits. Consider two qubits that are initially entangled but do not interact directly with one another. One of them is allowed to interact with an additional control qubit that is initially unentangled with the pair. Although this interaction is local, it can redistribute correlations among the three qubits and thereby change the entanglement remaining in the original two-qubit subsystem.

A basic example is a swap-type interaction. By exchanging the states of the system qubit and the control qubit, a full swap can transfer entanglement away from the original pair, converting a maximally entangled state into a separable one. Applying the inverse operation can restore the initial correlations, so the loss of entanglement is reversible when the control qubit remains accessible. Partial-swap operations produce intermediate behavior, continuously redistributing entanglement rather than removing it all at once. Thus, an apparent destruction or creation of bipartite entanglement may actually represent the transfer of correlations between different partitions of a larger system.

These examples also clarify the role of completely positive dynamical maps. A local, trace-preserving, completely positive operation acting on one member of an isolated bipartite system cannot increase a valid entanglement measure. Consequently, if an effective reduced description predicts that entanglement increases under a local process, the corresponding map cannot generally be interpreted as a completely positive channel acting on all possible input states. Such behavior may arise because the reduced map is defined only on a restricted set of states, because information retained in the control is used during the reverse process, or because correlations present at an intermediate stage invalidate the assumption of an initially factorized system and environment. The entanglement increase therefore does not amount to creating entanglement by an ordinary local quantum channel; instead, it reflects the recovery or redistribution of correlations stored in the enlarged system.

The same framework can be extended to irreversible dynamics. If the qubits are exposed to decay processes—such as amplitude damping, dephasing, or combinations of independent exponential-decay channels—the off-diagonal coherences and excited-state populations that support entanglement decrease with time. Although each individual decay rate may vary smoothly and exponentially, concurrence or negativity need not decay in the same asymptotic manner. For suitable initial mixed states and channel parameters, the evolving state can cross the boundary between entangled and separable states at a finite time. Entanglement then vanishes abruptly and remains zero even though some populations and coherences have not yet completely disappeared, a phenomenon commonly called entanglement sudden death.

Together, these qubit models distinguish reversible correlation transfer from genuinely irreversible entanglement loss. Controlled swap interactions show that local coupling to an accessible auxiliary system can move entanglement out of, and later back into, a chosen pair of qubits. Effective entanglement growth signals that the reduced evolution falls outside the standard description by a completely positive local map on an unrestricted state space. In contrast, combined decay channels can drive the system irreversibly into the separable region in finite time. Despite their simplicity, such models illustrate how strongly conclusions about entanglement depend on which degrees of freedom are retained, what initial correlations are allowed, and whether the reduced dynamics can be represented by a conventional quantum channel.
outputs.L5:
**The Simple One**

The world often asks us to become more: more successful, more certain, more impressive. Yet there is quiet strength in choosing the simple path.

One clear thought can calm a restless mind. One honest word can repair a broken trust. One small act of kindness can change the course of the day.

The simple things are not always easy, nor are they unimportant. They are the foundation beneath everything else—the breath before the answer, the hand held in silence, the courage to take one step.

Sometimes, one is enough. Sometimes, the simplest choice is the one that matters most.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the abstract of a paper about how local interactions with a control qubit can increase or decrease entanglement between two noninteracting qubits.
counterfactuals.output: The paper shows that entanglement between two noninteracting qubits can be controlled indirectly through local interactions with an auxiliary control qubit. By tuning these interactions and the control qubit’s state, the original qubits’ entanglement can either be enhanced or suppressed, providing a mechanism for manipulating quantum correlations without direct coupling between them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain, in one concise paragraph, examples where acting on only one member of an entangled qubit pair changes their entanglement, including the roles of swap operations, non-completely-positive maps, and finite-time disentanglement.
counterfactuals.output: A unitary acting only on one qubit—including a local bit flip or swapping that qubit with a local ancilla—cannot change total entanglement across the local–remote partition, although a swap can transfer the entanglement from the original qubit to the ancilla, making the original pair appear disentangled; likewise, swapping the two members globally merely relabels them. A genuinely local completely positive trace-preserving operation, such as measurement, dephasing, or amplitude damping, can reduce but not increase entanglement on average. By contrast, applying a non-completely-positive map to one qubit can mathematically produce increased or otherwise anomalous “entanglement,” but such a map is not a valid standalone physical operation on an arbitrarily entangled input and usually signals ignored initial correlations. Under sufficiently strong local noise, entanglement may reach exactly zero at a finite time—“entanglement sudden death”—even though each qubit’s coherence or populations decay only asymptotically.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an academic-style abstract describing two-qubit entanglement changes caused by interactions with an uncorrelated third qubit.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the evolution of entanglement between two qubits when one or both interact with a third qubit that is initially uncorrelated with the pair. Although the composite three-qubit system undergoes unitary dynamics, tracing out the auxiliary qubit produces an effectively nonunitary evolution of the two-qubit subsystem. Using concurrence and related bipartite entanglement measures, we characterize the redistribution of quantum correlations as functions of interaction strength, duration, and the initial states of the system and ancilla. The interaction can reduce, extinguish, preserve, or transiently revive the original two-qubit entanglement through the transfer of correlations to bipartite and genuinely tripartite sectors. In particular, entanglement loss is governed not only by decoherence-like mixing but also by monogamy constraints, while revivals arise from coherent information backflow from the third qubit. These results show that an initially independent ancillary qubit can substantially reshape two-qubit entanglement without carrying any initial correlations, highlighting the importance of controlled environmental degrees of freedom in quantum information processing and open-system dynamics.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: How can two noninteracting qubits evolve from a maximally entangled state to a separable state—or vice versa—when only one qubit interacts with a control? Also discuss complete positivity and exponential entanglement decay.
counterfactuals.output:
Let the two qubits be \(A\) and \(B\), and let only \(A\) interact with a control or environment \(C\). Although \(A\) and \(B\) do not interact directly, their entanglement can change because entanglement is redistributed among \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\).

For example, start with

\[
|\Phi^+\rangle_{AB}=\frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt2},
\qquad |c\rangle_C .
\]

A controlled interaction between \(A\) and \(C\) can produce

\[
|\Psi(t)\rangle_{ABC}
=\frac{|00\rangle_{AB}|c_0(t)\rangle_C+
|11\rangle_{AB}|c_1(t)\rangle_C}{\sqrt2}.
\]

After tracing out the control,

\[
\rho_{AB}(t)=\frac12\left(
|00\rangle\langle00|+|11\rangle\langle11|
+\gamma(t)|00\rangle\langle11|
+\gamma^*(t)|11\rangle\langle00|
\right),
\]

where

\[
\gamma(t)=\langle c_1(t)|c_0(t)\rangle .
\]

Its concurrence is

\[
C(t)=|\gamma(t)|.
\]

Thus:

- If \(|c_0\rangle=|c_1\rangle\), then \(C=1\): the qubits are maximally entangled.
- If the control states become orthogonal, \(\gamma=0\), and
  \[
  \rho_{AB}=\tfrac12(|00\rangle\langle00|+|11\rangle\langle11|),
  \]
  which is separable.
- If the control states later become indistinguishable again, entanglement revives.

The “lost” entanglement was not destroyed by an \(A\)-\(B\) interaction; it was transferred into correlations involving \(C\).

### Can a local operation create entanglement?

A deterministic local completely positive trace-preserving map cannot create entanglement from a genuinely separable state:

\[
\rho_{AB}=\sum_k p_k\,\rho_A^{(k)}\otimes\rho_B^{(k)}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(\Lambda_A\otimes I_B)(\rho_{AB})
\ \text{is separable}.
\]

Therefore, if \(AB\) appears separable at an intermediate time and later becomes entangled while only \(A\) interacts with \(C\), the intermediate reduced state \(\rho_{AB}\) is not the complete physical state. It is correlated with \(C\), which stores phase information or earlier entanglement. The later evolution cannot be represented as an autonomous CPTP map acting only on that intermediate \(\rho_{AB}\).

### Complete positivity

If at the initial time

\[
\rho_{ABC}(0)=\rho_{AB}(0)\otimes\rho_C,
\]

then the map from that initial time to any later time,

\[
\rho_{AB}(t)=
\operatorname{Tr}_C\!\left[
U_{AC}(t)(\rho_{AB}(0)\otimes\rho_C)U_{AC}^\dagger(t)
\right],
\]

is CPTP and local on \(A\). It can reduce entanglement but cannot create it from an initially separable \(AB\) state.

However, after \(A\) and \(C\) become correlated, a map from an intermediate time \(s\) to \(t\) need not be CP:

\[
\rho_{AB}(s)\not\mapsto \rho_{AB}(t)
\]

by a state-independent CPTP map. Entanglement revival is therefore associated with environmental memory or failure of CP divisibility, not necessarily with failure of complete positivity of the overall map from the original initial time.

### Exponential entanglement decay

For Markovian pure dephasing,

\[
\gamma(t)=e^{-\Gamma t},
\]

so for the Bell state above,

\[
C(t)=e^{-\Gamma t}.
\]

This gives smooth asymptotic entanglement decay. Exponential behavior typically follows from a time-homogeneous Markovian semigroup and a constant decay rate. Complete positivity alone does **not** require exponential decay. Depending on the interaction and environment, \(\gamma(t)\) may oscillate, revive, decay nonexponentially, or reach zero at finite time. Other noise models and mixed initial states can also produce “entanglement sudden death.”

In short: a local control can destroy bipartite entanglement by transferring it to the control; it can restore previously stored entanglement through memory effects, but it cannot create entanglement from a truly separable, control-uncorrelated state using only a local CPTP operation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a technical overview of a study demonstrating local control of bipartite entanglement, compensating entanglement changes under swaps, and “entanglement sudden death” produced by combining independent decay processes.
counterfactuals.output:
The study considers two initially entangled two-level systems—implemented, for example, by polarization-entangled photons—whose excitations decay into independent local environments. It shows that simple local “swap” operations can control the subsequent entanglement dynamics and that two individually smooth decay channels can jointly produce finite-time disentanglement.

### Model

A representative initial state is

\[
|\psi_0\rangle=\alpha |00\rangle+\beta |11\rangle,
\qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1 .
\]

Each subsystem undergoes an independent amplitude-damping channel,

\[
|0\rangle|0_E\rangle\rightarrow |0\rangle|0_E\rangle ,
\]

\[
|1\rangle|0_E\rangle\rightarrow
\sqrt{q_i}\,|1\rangle|0_E\rangle+
\sqrt{1-q_i}\,|0\rangle|1_E\rangle ,
\]

where \(q_i\) is the excitation-survival probability for subsystem \(i=A,B\). In a Markovian model, \(q_i(t)=e^{-\gamma_i t}\).

After tracing out the environments, the two-system density matrix remains an \(X\)-state. Its concurrence is

\[
C(t)=2\sqrt{q_Aq_B}\,
\max\!\left[
0,\,
|\alpha\beta|-|\beta|^2
\sqrt{(1-q_A)(1-q_B)}
\right].
\]

### Why independent decays produce sudden death

If only one subsystem decays, say \(q_B=1\), the subtractive term vanishes:

\[
C(t)=2|\alpha\beta|\sqrt{q_A}.
\]

Thus the entanglement decreases continuously and reaches zero only asymptotically.

When both independent channels act, populations appear in \(|01\rangle\) and \(|10\rangle\). In the concurrence formula, the geometric mean of these populations competes with the surviving \(|00\rangle\!\leftrightarrow |11\rangle\) coherence. For \(|\beta|>|\alpha|\), the threshold

\[
(1-q_A)(1-q_B)=\frac{|\alpha|^2}{|\beta|^2}
\]

is reached at a finite time. The concurrence then becomes exactly zero and remains zero: entanglement sudden death. For equal decay rates,

\[
t_{\rm ESD}
=-\frac{1}{\gamma}
\ln\!\left(1-\frac{|\alpha|}{|\beta|}\right).
\]

The result is notable because neither local reservoir needs to possess a sharp transition or non-Markovian behavior. Sudden death is generated by the nonlinear way in which entanglement depends on the output of the two independent processes.

### Local control using swaps

The control operations are local swaps or bit flips,

\[
X=|0\rangle\langle1|+|1\rangle\langle0|.
\]

A local unitary cannot change concurrence at the instant it is applied. It can, however, exchange populations between the decay-resistant ground state and the decay-sensitive excited state, thereby changing the state’s future trajectory under amplitude damping.

For example,

\[
(X\otimes X)(\alpha|00\rangle+\beta|11\rangle)
=\alpha|11\rangle+\beta|00\rangle .
\]

Thus the Schmidt coefficients are unchanged, but the larger coefficient may now multiply the stable \(|00\rangle\) component rather than the doubly excited component. This can:

- postpone or eliminate finite-time disentanglement;
- accelerate sudden death if the swap puts more weight in the vulnerable excitation sector;
- redirect which single-excitation populations are created;
- compensate the effect of an earlier swap through a later or complementary swap.

The timing is crucial. A swap made before substantial system-environment information has leaked out can strongly alter the remaining entanglement lifetime. A swap performed after concurrence has reached zero cannot recreate entanglement, because local unitaries cannot turn a separable state into an entangled one.

### Experimental interpretation

In optical realizations, polarization encodes the qubits, while interferometric paths or additional modes represent independent reservoirs. Wave plates implement the local \(X\) operations, and variable coupling to the ancillary modes sets \(q_A\) and \(q_B\). Two-qubit tomography then reconstructs the density matrix and concurrence.

The central conclusion is that local swaps do not directly add entanglement; instead, they rearrange the state relative to the preferred basis of local dissipation. This provides local control over entanglement lifetime and demonstrates that finite-time entanglement loss can be an emergent consequence of combining two otherwise ordinary, independent decay processes.
